pronunciation.approximation: BEL-ee — two syllables, stress on the first; the e is the open e of 'bed', never the long ay of 'bailey'.
pronunciation.note: Middle Welsh Beli (Beli mawr uab Manogan, 'Beli the Great, son of Manogan') is already written in the Latin alphabet, so the ASCII form loses nothing: the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule, since the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII drops. The traditional gloss 'bright, shining' reaches the name through its long-proposed connection with the Celtic god Belenos — conventionally derived from the root *bhel-, 'to shine' — but the etymology of Belenos itself is debated, and the handbooks record the link as a possibility, not a proof.

domains.title: The Root of the Pedigrees
domains.subtitle: The Island of Britain, the Four Sons, and the Question of the Bright One
domains.lead: Beli mawr — Beli the Great, son of Manogan — is the deep ancestor of British kingship: the king of the Island of Britain whom the Mabinogion sets at the head of its dynasties, father of Lludd, Caswallawn, Nynniaw, and Llefelys, and the name to which the medieval Welsh royal pedigrees climb. Behind the king, scholarship has long glimpsed a god — the continental Belenos, the 'bright, shining' one — but the texts give us the ancestor, and the ancestor is what the record can defend.

cards.name: The Island of Britain
cards.desc: Beli's realm in Lludd a Llefelys: the whole island, 'the crown of London' its seat — the deep past of a single British kingship.

cards.name: The Four Sons
cards.desc: Lludd, Caswallawn, Nynniaw — and, 'as the story tells', a fourth, Llefelys: the branches of the house the whole tradition descends from.

cards.name: The Pedigree
cards.desc: The Harleian genealogies carry the royal houses of Wales back to Beli Mawr — the name at the root of the British family trees.

cards.name: The Bright One
cards.desc: The proposed god behind the king: Belenos, 'bright, shining' — the continental name Tertullian and the Aquileia altars attest, linked to Beli by a long scholarly tradition.

mythology.lead: Beli has no adventure of his own: his story is his house. The Mabinogion knows him as the dead king whose four sons inherit Britain, France, and the quarrels of the next generation; the pedigrees know him as the root; and Geoffrey of Monmouth knows him as Heli, father of the builder of London.

myths.title: The Four Sons of Beli
myths.text:
The tale of Lludd and Llefelys opens with the settlement of the island: Beli the Great, son of Manogan, was king of this island, and he had three sons — Lludd, Caswallawn, and Nynniaw — and, as the story tells, a fourth son called Llefelys. When Beli died, the kingdom of the Island of Britain fell to Lludd as the eldest, and Lludd ruled it prosperously, rebuilding the walls of London and living there for most of the year. Llefelys, the youngest, went to France, won the love of the old king's only daughter, and inherited that kingdom in his turn.

What follows — the three plagues that fall on Britain, and Llefelys's counsel from the middle of the Channel — belongs to the sons' temples. Beli's part is finished in the opening lines, and that is precisely his function: he is the point from which legitimacy flows, the dead father whose reign makes his sons' divided world one family.

myths.title: Caswallawn's Veil
myths.text:
The Second Branch remembers Beli's house at the moment it takes the crown. While Brân the Blessed marched into Ireland to avenge Branwen, he left seven men as regents in Britain, his son Caradog at their head. Caswallawn son of Beli marched against them wearing a veil of illusion, so that no one could see him — only his sword killing. He slew the seven, and Caradog died of a broken heart at the sight of the slaughter and the knowledge of who held the island now.

Caswallawn son of Beli became king in London. The branch never explains or excuses the usurpation; it simply registers that while the children of Llŷr spent themselves overseas, the children of Beli took the island — the two great houses of Welsh tradition passing the crown between them without a battle anyone could see.

myths.title: The Root of the Royal Trees
myths.text:
Outside the tales, the record that made Beli matter was parchment of a drier kind. The Harleian genealogies — the collection of Welsh royal pedigrees preserved in British Library, Harley MS 3859 (c. 1100) — carry the lines of the British kingdoms back generation by generation until they reach Beli mawr, who stands near the root of the trees. To claim a throne in early Wales was, in part, to publish a pedigree, and the pedigrees converge on him.

The convention was old and tenacious: centuries later, the genealogical tracts still counted descent from Beli the Great as the deepest legitimacy a Welsh royal house could print. He is the standing proof that in the British tradition, ancestry is not decoration on kingship — it is the thing itself.

myths.title: Heli, Father of Lud
myths.text:
Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136) took the Welsh Beli into Latin and made him a chapter of world history. As Heli he reigns after King Cligueillus, a man of forty years' rule, and fathers three sons: Lud, Cassibelaunus, and Nennius. Lud succeeds him and rebuilds the city of Trinovantum with noble walls, surrounding it with countless towers and renaming it Kaerlud, Lud's City — whence, Geoffrey says, its later name London, and the memory of the king in the gate called Ludgate.

Through Geoffrey, Beli's house entered the bloodstream of European letters: the Historia was one of the most copied books of the Middle Ages, and the sons of Heli — Lud the city-builder, Cassibelaunus the enemy of Caesar — carried their father's ancestry wherever Latin was read.

myths.title: The Bright One Behind the King
myths.text:
Older than any Welsh manuscript is a continental witness the scholars keep setting beside Beli's name. Around the year 200, Tertullian lists the local gods of the provinces and gives the Noricans Belenus (Apologeticum 24); a generation later, Herodian tells how, at the siege of Aquileia in 238, the citizens credited their deliverance to Apollo, the god the people of that region worshipped under the name Belis. The altars agree: dedications Belino Augusto sacrum cluster at Aquileia and across the eastern Alpine provinces.

Whether the Welsh ancestor-king descends from this 'bright, shining' god is the standing question of Beli scholarship. The names are close, the traditional gloss fits, and a euhemerized god makes a plausible root for a genealogy — but no text performs the identification, and the honest verdict is the one the handbooks give: a venerable possibility, unproven. This temple holds the question open.

lore.syncretism: Beli's whole cross-cultural argument is the Belenos question. The continental god is attested from Aquileia to Noricum, glossed by the ancients as a Celtic Apollo, and derived by tradition from *bhel-, 'to shine'. Welsh Beli Mawr matches the name nearly perfectly, and from O'Rahilly onward scholars have set the Irish ancestor-god Bile beside both, proposing a single Celtic 'bright one' dimmed into three literatures as three ancestors. Mac Cana and Koch record the comparison; neither certifies it. The distinction worth keeping is Geoffrey's other Belinus — the son of Dunvallo, brother of Brennius — a different figure who shares nothing with Beli Mawr but the name. Within the Welsh corpus, Beli's closest kin are the other fountainheads of dynasty: [[don|Dôn]], mother of the Children of Dôn, and Llŷr, father of the house of Llŷr, whose sons Brân and [[manawydan|Manawydan]] lose the island's crown to Beli's son Caswallawn in the Second Branch.
lore.culturalLegacy: Beli's afterlife is genealogical before it is literary. The medieval pedigrees made descent from Beli Mawr the deepest claim a British dynasty could print, and the convention outlived the Middle Ages: Tudor and Stuart antiquaries, eager to trace the crown to British and Trojan roots, found Beli waiting at the root of the trees Geoffrey had Latinized. Through Geoffrey's Heli he fathered the legend of London itself — Lud's town, Lud's gate, the name written into the city's streets — and through his son Cassibelaunus he stands two generations above Shakespeare's Cymbeline, whose Britain is still Beli's island. In modern Wales the name persists quietly: Beli remains a Welsh personal name, and Beli Mawr keeps his place in the national memory as the grandfather of kings. Modern Celtic pagan and Druid practice honors the ancestral Belenus beside him, keeping the old question — king or bright god — alive rather than answered.
lore.extendedMeditation: Beli is the patron of everything that matters most and does least: the dead father, the founding reign, the name at the root of the tree. He fights no monster, wins no bride, casts no spell; the Mabinogion finishes him in a sentence, and then builds a world on him. His sons inherit his island and quarrel over it; his house takes the crown under a veil of illusion; the pedigrees spend a thousand years climbing back to him. That is how ancestry actually works — the founder is never the hero of the story, only its premise. Beli asks the genealogist's hard question of every institution and every family: not what have you done, but what are you descended from, and does the root still hold. And the name itself holds its own question: whether the bright one, the shining god of the continental altars, lies behind the sober Welsh king. Some roots run deeper than the record can follow. Beli is the place where Britain's goes dark.
lore.originalScriptNote: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Beli (Beli mawr uab Manogan) in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, and the ASCII spelling loses nothing — hence Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: beli.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Beli is a textual figure: no inscription, image, or votive object from Britain names him, and no cult site is his. His witnesses are codices — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410) for the Mabinogion tales, and British Library Harley MS 3859 (c. 1100) for the genealogies that root the Welsh dynasties in him. The material evidence belongs to his proposed continental cognate: the dedications Belino Augusto sacrum from Aquileia and the eastern Alps are real stones with a real theonym — the strongest archaeological fact in the whole dossier, and the reason the 'bright, shining' gloss will not go away. Comparative evidence only: no altar can be read as addressed to the Welsh ancestor-king himself.
